content: After 2016, faculty members from Makerere University in Kampala, Uganda, attended a capacity-building training program on adolescent health. This training, hosted by the Namibian government, was part of the WHO strategy to enhance institutional capacity for leadership and training in adolescent health across East and Southern Africa. Following this, postgraduate training in adolescent health increased significantly. By 2018, a dedicated six-week course on adolescent health was introduced for second-year residents pursuing a Master’s in Paediatrics and Child Health, replacing the previous allocation of only six hours. This course includes lectures, practical training, and outreach activities. During their six-week rotation in adolescent health and medicine, postgraduate students engage in school outreach programs and provide care to adolescent patients, fostering their role as advocates for adolescent health care. The next step in Uganda involved integrating adolescent health content into pre-service education and training. This process began with a needs assessment and curriculum review for the Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery programs. It revealed that key departments, such as Paediatrics, Nursing, Obstetrics and Gynaecology, and Psychiatry, allocated minimal time to adolescent health topics. Consequently, a comprehensive outline of topics for a trainer program was developed. Faculty and resource persons were trained to deliver updated content using interactive teaching techniques, resulting in 15 master trainers. In June 2019, an extracurricular undergraduate course on adolescent health, comprising 20 hours of training, was launched. Since then, over 400 students, including undergraduates and master’s students in various disciplines, have received training in adolescent health. To provide practical skills, the Friday Adolescent Clinic and its partners organized biannual skills-building sessions for adolescents. The clinic, established in May 2013 at Mulago National Referral Hospital, serves as a general adolescent clinic and has provided care to over 8,000 adolescents and young adults. These sessions offer adolescents a platform to learn life skills, share experiences, and pursue their goals while allowing trainees in the Master’s program to practice skill-building among adolescents. Globally, since 2015, countries have utilized the WHO-developed Global Standards for Quality Health Care Services for Adolescents to improve the accessibility and quality of adolescent health services. These standards focus on adolescent health literacy, community support, service packages, provider competencies, facility characteristics, adolescent participation, equity, and data-driven quality improvements. However, monitoring the implementation of these standards has traditionally required time-intensive and costly surveys. To address this, WHO developed a web-based platform for digital monitoring and evaluation of national quality standards. Ghana was an early adopter, piloting the platform in six facilities in 2019. School nurses were equipped with mobile tablets and internet access to facilitate regular use of the platform. The implementation process included adapting global standards to the national context, orienting stakeholders, and training staff. Within three months, six facilities had collected data on care quality from over 3,000 adolescents and healthcare staff. The platform’s implementation improved communication, professional competencies, and standardized tools, while increasing awareness of adolescents’ unique health needs. In the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the government has been working to improve access to quality sexual and reproductive health (SRH) services for adolescents and youth. Despite adolescents comprising a significant portion of the population, only 17% utilized health services in 2021. To address this, WHO supported a collaborative learning project aimed at improving service quality. Service providers worked together to identify and solve common problems, strengthening their capacity and attitudes to enhance adolescent health services. The project, launched in 2018-2019, covered six districts and involved training sessions and the development of high-quality materials for providers. Initial results showed increased youth attendance and satisfaction with services, prompting plans to scale up the approach to 25 zones across five provinces. School health services (SHS) have been operational in many countries for decades, providing health and well-being services to students. Schools, with their high attendance rates, offer a unique platform to deliver these services and reach underserved, low-income, and high-risk populations.
